linguistic.morphology.name: Morphology
linguistic.morphology.values.agglutinati: Words are built by stacking affixes one after another, where each affix carries exactly one meaning. The pieces stay clearly recognizable, like building blocks snapped together.
linguistic.morphology.values.fusional.de: Words change their form through endings and prefixes that bundle multiple grammatical meanings at once. A single ending might express gender, number, and case simultaneously, making the pieces hard to pull apart.
linguistic.morphology.values.introflexiv: Grammar is built into the word from the inside: a root of consonants carries the core meaning, while different vowel patterns woven through it create new words. For example, the Arabic root k-t-b relates to writing, and kataba, kitāb, and kātib all come from it.
linguistic.morphology.values.isolating.d: Words typically consist of single morphemes and don't change their form. Grammar is expressed through word order and separate function words rather than endings or prefixes.
linguistic.morphology.values.polysynthet: A single word can express what other languages would say in a whole sentence, by fusing the verb, subject, object, and other elements together. Common in indigenous languages of the Americas and the Arctic.
